exampleAnswers.title: Finding the Sine or Cosine of a Special Angle Given in Degrees

question.explanation:
Let's remind ourselves of the special trigonometric ratios, as given by the unit circle.

From the unit circle, we see that the angle $210^\circ$ corresponds to the point $\left( -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, -\dfrac{1}{2} \right).$

Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the $y$-coordinate, we have $\sin 210^\circ = -\dfrac{1}{2}.$

exampleAnswers.title: Finding the Secant or Cosecant of a Special Angle

question.explanation:
Let's remind ourselves of the special trigonometric ratios, as given by the unit circle.

From the unit circle, we see that the angle $225^\circ$ corresponds to the point $\left( -\dfrac{\sqrt 2}{2}, -\dfrac{\sqrt 2}{2} \right).$

Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the $y$-coordinate, we have $\sin 225^\circ= -\dfrac{\sqrt 2}{2}.$

Therefore, using the fact that $\csc{\theta} = \dfrac{1}{\sin\theta},$ we have

\[ \csc 225^\circ= \dfrac{1}{\sin{225^\circ }} = -\dfrac 2{\sqrt 2}=-\sqrt{2}. \]

example.title: Finding the Secant or Cosecant of a Special Angle

question.explanation:
Let's remind ourselves of the special trigonometric ratios, as given by the unit circle.

From the unit circle, we see that the angle $\dfrac{7\pi}{6}$ corresponds to the point $\left( -\dfrac{\sqrt 3}{2}, -\dfrac{1}{2} \right).$

Since the cosine of the angle corresponds to the $x$-coordinate, we have $\cos\left( \dfrac {7\pi} {6}\right) = -\dfrac{\sqrt 3}{2}.$

Therefore, using the fact that $\sec{\theta} = \dfrac{1}{\cos\theta},$ we have

\[ \sec\left(\dfrac{7\pi}{6}\right) = \dfrac{1}{\cos{\left(\dfrac{7\pi}{6}\right) }} = -\dfrac{2}{\sqrt 3} = -\dfrac{2\sqrt 3}{3}. \]

exampleAnswers.title: Finding the Tangent or Cotangent of a Special Angle

question.explanation:
Let's remind ourselves of the special trigonometric ratios, as given by the unit circle.

From the unit circle, we see that the angle $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ corresponds to the point $\left( \dfrac{1}{2}, \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \right).$

  • Since the cosine of the angle corresponds to the $x$-coordinate, we have $\cos\left( \dfrac {\pi} {3}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}.$

  • Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the $y$-coordinate, we have $\sin\left( \dfrac {\pi} {3}\right) = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.$

Therefore, using the fact that $\cot{\theta} = \dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta},$ we have

\[ \cot\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = \dfrac{\cos{\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) }}{\sin{\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) }} = \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)}{\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}. \]

From the unit circle, we see that the angle $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ corresponds to the point $\left( \dfrac{1}{2}, \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \right).$

  • Since the cosine of the angle corresponds to the $x$-coordinate, we have $\cos\left( \dfrac {\pi} {3}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}.$

  • Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the $y$-coordinate, we have $\sin\left( \dfrac {\pi} {3}\right) = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.$

Therefore, using the fact that $\tan{\theta} = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta},$ we have

\[ \tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = \dfrac{\sin{\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) }}{\cos{\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) }} = \dfrac{\left(\dfrac {\sqrt{3}} 2\right)}{\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)} = \sqrt{3}. \]
